newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan myth of safe, secure nation shattered.
newsitem.headline: Japan myth of safe, secure nation shattered.

text.p: The Kobe earthquake, a subway gas attack and a deadly food poisoning epidemic have shattered the myth of Japan as a safe and secure nation, a government report said on Tuesday.

Social changes, such as a rapidly ageing population, a dwindling birthrate and the end of life-long employment practices, are also causing insecurity and changing the perceptions Japanese held about their country, according to the report on Japanese life.
"The Japanese have long believed that they had created a nation which was safe, secure and economically affluent. This has also been accepted internationally," the report said.

"But in recent years, a shadow of doubt has been cast over the safety and security of Japanese society and the faith in the system behind it," said the report issued by the government's Economic Planning Agency.
Japan has boasted economic and social stability which has been brought about by a well-educated population hired by companies which believed in jobs for life.
The stable incomes, in turn, have helped to keep the crime rate and the number of divorces and single-parent families low, the report said.
Several natural disasters and the government's reaction to them have also shaken Japan's self-image.
This year, a mass food poisoning outbreak caused by the O-157 colon bacillus claimed 11 lives and made more than 9,000 ill nationwide. Health officials have not discovered the cause.
The Kobe earthquake in January 1995 and the feeble government response to it proved that Japan was ill-equipped to cope with natural disasters.
Compared to the 1994 earthquake in Los Angeles, five times more buildings were damaged and the death toll of more than 6,300 was more than 100 times as high as in Los Angeles, the report said.
The safety myth was exploded by the March 1995 nerve gas attack on the Tokyo subway system, which killed 12 and left more than 5,000 ill when sarin nerve gas was released on the trains.
Members of the Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) are now on trial for the attack. A sect member is also suspected of shooting Japan's top police official last year.
Though Japan remains safe from violent crimes compared to other countries, a rise in illegal gun possession is also eroding the security Japan used to know, the report said.
Worsening employment conditions among young people can also lead to increased crime rates, it said.
Companies have cut staffing levels and held back pay hikes to survive the years of recession after the collapse of the late 1980s economic "bubble" of inflated stock and land prices.

Fearing they might be next in line to be fired, employees are relying more on their skills to secure a stable income, whereas before they used to rely on the company they worked for to take care of them until retirement.
The rapidly ageing population is also worrisome, especially given the poor condition of state finances, as a growing number of pensioners will be relying on fewer and fewer workers to support them.
The report called for reforms in the social security system, especially in medical care.

The report also called for a flexible wage system which would facilitate employment for the elderly. Many companies still use a traditional wage system where workers with more seniority are paid more than their younger colleagues.
